transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players will be able to convert this position, but only a true genius would have been able to win with four brilliant moves. But now, after the king creates an escape, even if we try to double up the rooks, the king is going to go to the center and there is no checkmate. If you try to sacrifice the knight with knight to f6 check, the king is not going to go to the corner allowing this checkmate. Instead, after pawn takes and queen h5, black is going f8 again [music] and after this, the king once again runs to safety and there is no checkmate. During the game, I was trying to make queen h5 work with the idea of threatening checkmate. And if black pushes h6, I thought, well, knight f6 and once the pawn takes, we take here and this is an unstoppable checkmate, either like this or like this. But then I realized that after h6 and knight f6 check, the king can simply go to h8. And now, black seems to be just out of the woods, but what I failed to see is that [music] knight f6 is actually the start of a checkmating attack and it is the first of four brilliant moves. Because after king to h8, white has the incredible and beautiful queen g5. A move that is so subtle and yet so brilliant. The idea of queen g5 is that now this pawn is pinned to the king and we are preparing a rook sacrifice. For example, if black plays any random move, we're simply going to take and take like this with a full checkmate. Meaning that black is only left with knight to g4. And now, we could happily take the free knight and leave it at that, but we can actually follow up with rook takes h6, another brilliancy. And after the knight takes, we bring the other rook to h1 and it's the same thing. This knight is pinned and the king is completely paralyzed. None of these pieces can stop what's to come. So, after any random move, we're going to sacrifice the other rook. And once the pawn takes, queen takes h6 is a beautiful checkmate.
